implementation_notes: The data class is Kotlin's replacement for the accessor-filled bean: one declaration generates the constructor, componentN, copy, equals/hashCode and toString, while the kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin derives a KSerializer from @Serializable, so the same DTO works on JVM, JS and Native without reflection. The carrier is therefore native and only the serialization is library-supplied; Jackson with the Kotlin module is the alternative when the surrounding stack is Java-first. Data classes stay shallowly immutable, so collections should be exposed read-only and validation belongs in an init block.
code_sketch:
@Serializable
data class OrderDto(val id: Long, val customer: String, val lines: List<LineDto> = emptyList())

val wire = Json.encodeToString(OrderDto(1, "Ada"))
val back = Json.decodeFromString<OrderDto>(wire)
pitfalls: kotlinx.serialization rejects unknown keys by default and writes defaults only when configured (encodeDefaults): a missing field raises MissingFieldException while a defaulted field can vanish from the wire, so defaults and @Required must be deliberate.
Data classes give structural equality and copy() but not deep immutability: a val property pointing at a MutableList can still be mutated.
The compiler plugin is required at build time and only kotlinx-aware or reflection/Jackson-based serializers work; a plain Java serializer cannot handle Kotlin classes without the Kotlin module.
